forms.description: The body everything else sits on, and the element that draws them. Parts outside a device stay plain HTML.

Four screws, one in each corner of the device, each with its drive at its own angle. `screws` says which: a head (`pan`, `countersunk`, `button`, `cheese`), a drive (`slot`, `cross`, `hex`, `star`) and a size (`M2`, `M3`, `M4`), slotted M2 pan heads if it's bare.
The primitive everything else can be built from, in plain HTML.
Parts that belong together, with no body: one canvas between them, however many there are. A part on its own needs no such thing.
An LCD panel sunk in a black frame. Its text shows in the ink of `material`.

`
12:34
`. The text is real, so it reads out and copies, and a space is a blank digit. `bare` leaves off its panel and glass, for digits that are part of whatever they sit on. `slant` leans them, degrees. `point-cell` gives a decimal point a digit's place of its own, as on displays where it's a separate LED.

`<d-seg name box stroke lean stems>` children are digits, and `<d-seg name box path viewbox>` or `<d-seg name box text weight>` fixed shapes, `box` being x y w h in mm from the glass's corner. `on` lists what's driven: a digit as `name=5`, or `name=*` for every stroke, and a shape by its name. `ghost` shows what's off, 0 to 1, as a slant of the light does. `light` is a lamp beside the glass at `light-at` in mm, spreading `light-size` mm across, in `color`.

`
SPELL
`: an alphanumeric tube, each character out of fourteen strokes, as on a vacuum fluorescent display. The text is real, and fills from the left. `weight` is a stroke's width as a share of the character's height, and `slant` leans it, degrees. It has no panel of its own: it sits under whatever glass holds it.
Numerals made of wire, glowing inside glass tubes, one tube per character.
A departure board. Flaps run through the alphabet to reach each new letter.
Number wheels behind a window, with each one carrying into the next.

`
HELLO
`. Each dot is one LED, and `scroll` runs anything too long to fit past the window.
Lit text set straight onto a panel, such as a clock showing through glass.
d-readout="seven" lights too hard for numerals this tall: the bloom comes back as blocks around each digit.

`<d-screen kind="crt" live><canvas width="160" height="120"></canvas></d-screen>`. `kind` is crt, led, lcd, oled, tft, eink or coat. Draw on the canvas however you like: one canvas pixel is one pixel, LED or scanline. A coat gives no light: it's a film on the back of glass, its `material` lit by the room, its `text` colour what's behind, and the canvas how much of it is left. A video or image works too. `mono` makes a crt a monochrome tube, one even phosphor, and `bulge` is how far its picture bows. An lcd takes `response`, ms for a pixel to turn, and `rate`, the panel's frames a second while it does. Any panel's `active` is the size of its pixels' area in mm, the rest being bare panel or dark glass. `backlight` is a lamp colour, on with `lit`, `glow` strong, and `wash` how far it colours the panel, 0 to 1. `pointer` says what's on it draws its own pointer, so the page's goes away over it. An led wall takes `cabinet`, the width and height of the panels it's built of in mm, and shows the seams between them. Or put real elements on it: `<d-screen kind="lcd"><canvas width="640" height="400"></canvas><form>...</form></d-screen>`. One element, which fills the panel, laid out by the browser and live as ever, and shown through the panel at the canvas's pixels, or with `pitch`, mm between pixels, at as many as fit the panel at any size. It's written as it should look, dark on light on a panel lit by the room, light on dark on one that gives light. With no canvas it gets one, a pixel to a css px.
Words cut into what it's on. `d-mark="label flat"` prints them flat, and `ink` sets the colour.

What a die stamps: an ``, or the words inside, in `material`. What's see-through in an image stays off it, so any picture can be foil. A symbol from the icon set, printed on what it's on, as big as its box: `icon` says which and `color` its ink. `weight` is its stroke, on the icon's 24 unit grid.
A raised plate with its text engraved. `rivets` adds one at each end.
Punched label tape: raised letters, whitened where the plastic stretched.

Letters set round a circle, on whatever is under them. `text` runs clockwise from `start` degrees, or is centred on `at` degrees, and `radius` is mm to their middles. `under` sets it for reading along the bottom of the circle, running the other way with its tops to the middle. `height` casts the letters to stand that many mm, in place of engraving them.
`d-mark="print pad"`, or offset, silk, etch, mould, foil, emboss, deboss or spray, around text, or `path` and `viewbox`.

`<div d-mark="sticker" material lift corner rotate border>`: a thin sheet stuck on, with its text in `color`. `d-mark="sticker card"` is stiff card instead: it lies flat on the highest thing under it and can hang past the edge, and `rim` runs a band of its own material round the outside of `border`, in mm. `path` die-cuts it, and `lift` needs a plain rectangle. `border` is the white margin a die leaves round the print, in mm: what's printed is then ink on the sheet, not the sheet.
A field of holes in the surface, `pitch` apart and `hole` across, in mm. `square` makes them square, and `round` keeps them inside a circle.

Slots milled in a row, for air or sound. The row runs along the longer side. `rotate` turns the row about its middle, degrees, and `wall` is how far out a chamfer runs round each slot, mm. `recess` moulds each slot instead: a crisp-edged stadium that wide, mm, its floor the shell's own, falling from `deep` / 3 at one side to `deep`, mm, at the other, and there the slit, `slot` wide. The slit runs `run` of the way along, and the first `blind` of the row have none, for the ones with nothing behind them.
A pressed speaker disc: a whole circle of holes, which d-opening="grille" cannot do.
A speaker cone. `level` pushes it out, 0 to 1.
A thin sunk line that fills its box.

A camera lens: a black well behind coated elements. All of them fill the opening, so no element has an edge you can see, and the room shows once on each, at its own size and turned over on the hollow one, in the colour its coating leaves at that angle. Glass is nearly black where it faces nothing bright, so those images are all the colour it has, and they're what makes a lens read as deep. `rim` is how much of the radius the outer ring takes, `pupil` how much the glass does, `core` how much of the glass the iris leaves open, `height` how far it stands, mm, and `baffles` how many ridges step down the well to the glass.
A pane laid over what is inside it. The form says which.
A pane laid over what is inside it. The form says which.
A pane laid over what is inside it. The form says which.

A flat coated window into a body, as on a viewfinder or a meter: a pane of its own over what's inside, which keeps its colour and texture, and a reflection of the room in the colour the coating leaves. `film` is the coating, 0 for bare glass, `coat` how much it shows, `radius` its corners, mm, and `height` how far it stands over what's inside, mm. `material` is what it's made of, glass unless it says otherwise, as a moulded polycarbonate window does.
A clear round dome over what's under it, as wide as its box. Goes after what it covers.
A camera flash: a stepped plastic lens over a yellow phosphor, behind a flush window.
With `bar` it's a compact camera's xenon flash: a long window ribbed into a fresnel, over a reflector with the tube lying along it.

A crystal over everything so far, the shape of its box, or `path` in `viewbox`. `square` as for a bezel. `material` is what it's made of, `mineral-glass` unless it's `sapphire` or `acrylic`, which sets how much it reflects. `coat` is how much less it shines if it's bloomed. `chamfer` is the cut round its top edge, `width angle` in mm and degrees, which is what shows a flat crystal is there. `lens` is a small magnifier on it, as `x y w h` in mm from its middle, and `zoom` how strong that is.
A row of socket pins, as on the edge of a dev board: square holes on a 2.54mm pitch, as many as fit its long side.

A socket on the side of something. The form says which. A jack takes `nut`, the hex nut of a panel jack, and `plug`, a lead plugged in, whose barrel is that material. It may wrap a checkbox, for the plug to come and go.

A socket on the side of something. The form says which. A jack takes `nut`, the hex nut of a panel jack, and `plug`, a lead plugged in, whose barrel is that material. It may wrap a checkbox, for the plug to come and go.

A socket on the side of something. The form says which. A jack takes `nut`, the hex nut of a panel jack, and `plug`, a lead plugged in, whose barrel is that material. It may wrap a checkbox, for the plug to come and go.

A socket on the side of something. The form says which. A jack takes `nut`, the hex nut of a panel jack, and `plug`, a lead plugged in, whose barrel is that material. It may wrap a checkbox, for the plug to come and go.

A socket on the side of something. The form says which. A jack takes `nut`, the hex nut of a panel jack, and `plug`, a lead plugged in, whose barrel is that material. It may wrap a checkbox, for the plug to come and go.

The mouth of a floppy drive, filling its box. A shallow step in the case with slanted walls, tall at the right end where a thumb reaches the disk, a pale door set further back there, the slit running through both, and a pinhole for a paper clip.
The mouth of a cartridge slot, filling its box: a square-cut step in the case with a slit along the middle of its floor. There's nothing to press, since a cartridge is pushed straight in.
A port seen from above, cut into the very edge of the case.
A panel-mounted BNC socket. The checkbox says whether a cable is plugged in.
A shrouded 4mm socket, as a meter's leads go in: a black collar standing proud, and in it a coloured insert round a deep hole with a brass contact down it. `material` is the insert.
A binding post from above: a stem standing `height` mm with a knurled head you screw down on a wire. The box is the head.
A strip of LEDs behind a diffuser. `value` is how far along it is lit, 0 to 1.

A moving-coil needle and nothing else, to swing over a face printed with d-mark="scale": a panel meter's, whatever its scale says. It jumps and overshoots, as a light movement does. `pivot` is where it turns, as `x y` in mm from the box's corner, the middle of the box unless it's somewhere else, as one below the window is. `length` is mm from there to the tip, to the box's edge by default, `hub` how much of that near the pivot is left out, for a hood to hide, and `from` and `to` are its ends in degrees clockwise from straight up. `width` is how wide it is at its foot and `height` how far it stands, both mm, and `color` overrides its material's.

`
`. `flush` sets its bezel in flat, chamfered, in place of the rolled rim.

A panel meter: a moving coil behind a clear square front, its needle swinging through 90 degrees from a pivot low on a white face. `ticks` and `minor` set the scale as on a gauge, `label` prints the unit, and `material` is the face. Spec: a 60mm square front with about a 45mm scale radius, as on a common DIN panel ammeter.
A backlit level meter, its needle swinging from a pivot hidden below the window.
A row of segments. The top of the range shows amber, then red. `from="end"` fills it from the far end instead.
A wall clock. Follows the computer's clock, or `time="10:08:30"` if set.
A compass card floating on a heading, in degrees.
A ring that closes as the value rises.
A printed tuning scale on black glass, lit from behind while the radio plays.

The hands of a travel clock, in a box as wide as the dial. Follows the computer's clock, or `time="10:08:30"`. Wraps a range input of minutes round twelve hours, which sets the alarm hand: drag it round.

A paper tuning scale behind a narrow window, running down it, and a needle that follows `value`, 0 to 1. `d-meter="strip open"` has no paper: the needle and pane run over a scale printed on the recess it sits in. `needle` is the needle's material.

A screw head, drawn to fill its box. `head` is `pan`, `countersunk`, `button` or `cheese`, `drive` is `slot`, `cross`, `hex` or `star`, and `angle` turns the drive, in degrees. Its proportions are the ISO ones for the nearest size to the box. `socket` is a hex drive.

A moulded corner on a covered cabinet, as on an amp or a flight case, with a stud through it. `at` says which corner of the box is the cabinet's: `tl`, `tr`, `bl` or `br`. `height` is mm, `stud` the stud's material.
A turned stack on an upright axis, seen from the side, its foot on the bottom of its box. `profile` is each step going up, diameter and height in mm.

A rewind crank folded down on its knob: a short turned drum on a shaft leaning `tilt` degrees, tipped towards you so its top shows as an ellipse, with the crank lying across that and its handle sprung into a notch at the rim. The box is the drum's width by all you see of it, `wall` is its side in mm.
A round cap screwed in flush, with a knurled ring to turn it by and `inset` in the middle.
A flat lug with a round hole, to take a strap ring. It stands off the side of a body, its hole at the outer end. `side` is left or right.
The domed head of a rivet, filling its box.
A staple through a stack of card, seen from its crown: flat wire, and the dent it pulls in the card round it. It runs along its box.
A length of piano hinge laid along an edge: a barrel of rolled knuckles the whole length of its box. `pitch` is mm from knuckle to knuckle.

A split ring, two turns of flat wire seen from above, filling its box. `from` and `to` are degrees clockwise from the right, for a ring that passes through something: draw it twice, either side of what it goes through.
A flat tab of steel with a hole through it, standing out of whatever it's riveted into. Its hole is at the far end of its box.
A socket head sunk in a steel collar, as a shell is screwed together from the front.
The plain key. A value on the tag picks another form, as `d-key="chiclet"`.
A big round button, sat in a collar. Lights up with `on`, and while it is held. `gain` sets how bright its lamp burns. Its cap is dished for a finger, or swells by `crown` mm for a palm.

A flush round button with a metal collar, as on a lift panel. `on` lights the legend, and `gain` sets how bright its lamp burns. With `aria-pressed` it stays in while that says so, as a release does while what it lets go is turned.

A latching bar, one of a row: a radio button or checkbox in a label, a link, which stays in at the page it goes to, or a button with `aria-pressed`. `color` lights the bar while it is latched, and the device's `backlight` lights its legend whether it is or not. A dark print stops light, so it never glows. `d-key="tab lit"` is a bar that lights right through while it's latched, with its legend left black on it, so the one that's in reads the same in any room. `gain` turns its legend and its light up, and `gap` is how much of the well shows round the cap.
A laptop key: low, square, with its legend and edges lit from under the cap.

A mechanical keycap: tall, on a long travel, lit from the switch below. `profile` is the family it's cut to, `cherry`, `oem`, `sa`, `dsa` or `xda`, which sets how tall it stands, how big its top is and how it's dished. `dish` overrides that (`cylindrical`, `spherical` or `flat`), `row` sculpts it as that row of a board, 1 at the top to 4, and `legend` says how its legend is put on: `pad`, `twoshot`, `laser` or `engraved`.

A round gamepad button, domed, with its letter under a clear cap. `rise` is how far it stands up, mm, and `color` tints the letter. `flat` turns the dome into a moulded disc with a rolled edge, and `gap` is the mm between it and its hole. `plate` prints a disc of that colour under the letter, `plate-size` of the way across, and `ink` colours the letter. `icon` prints an icon in place of one.

A flat key with square shoulders, in a narrow gap, that goes down onto a hard stop. The text inside is its legend. `open` names the sides with no gap, `left`, `right`, `top` or `bottom`, for a key that runs to the edge of what holds it. `lamp` sets a pin LED in it, near the top, which `on` lights. `collar` is a metal frame round it. `round` makes it a disc, and `path` in a `viewbox` any other outline, traced off a cap that isn't a box, as a calculator's barrel keys.

A printed patch on a sheet of film, over a snap dome. There's no gap and no key, so all that moves is the film, which dips under a finger and stays pillowed a little over the dome at rest. The text inside is its legend, and children are printed on it.

A tactile switch on a board, seen from above: a square body under a steel cover, and the stem that pushes the dome, which travels a quarter of a millimetre and clicks. Sized to the part: 6mm and 12mm are the common ones. `cap` snaps a cap over the stem, `round` or `square`, in its `material`. Spec: 6 × 6 body with a 3.5mm stem, 12 × 12 with a 7mm one, 0.25mm travel.

An emergency stop: a mushroom head on a collar that locks down when struck and stays down until it's let out, as the checkbox inside does, or `aria-pressed` on a button. It sits on a yellow plate, and its text is its name, not printed. `grip` ribs the head's rim (`ribbed` or `smooth`), and `plate` names the plate's material. Spec: a 40mm head on a 22mm hole, about 6mm of stroke.
A capacitive key: printed on the glass, lit when held, and left on with `on`.
A fingerprint pad. Hold it until the ring closes and it fires a `hold` event, by finger or Space.
A steel push button with a lit ring round its cap. `on` lights the ring.
A capacitive key with a picture for a legend, printed in the glass and lit from behind. Nothing goes down on glass, so its press is the light coming up, and it still gives a tap.

A key that stands out of the edge of a case and goes in sideways, ribbed across its end. `d-key="edge right"` or `"edge top"`, and the box is as much of it as stands out. On a label round a checkbox it stays in, as a tape key does.

A key that stands out of the edge of a case and goes in sideways, ribbed across its end. `d-key="edge right"` or `"edge top"`, and the box is as much of it as stands out. On a label round a checkbox it stays in, as a tape key does.

A silicone key that glows from under the rubber. A checkbox inside makes it latch. `material` is its rubber and `height` how far it stands, mm, `radius` its corners, mm, and `gap` the mm to what holds it. With `through` the LED lights the whole of a pale key, and not a slit, and `level`, 0 to 1, dims it.
A release seen from the side: a threaded button pressed straight down into a collar. `travel` is mm.

A rocker on the shoulder, tucked under the edge of the shell. `d-key="bumper left"` or `"bumper right"`. Plain, it's a straight bar set at an angle. `moulded` follows the shoulder, drawn in millimetres.
The button in the middle: smoked black, with `logo`, an SVG path on a 2 by 2 box round 0, lit from behind while it's on.
A rubber pill coming up through a slot in a shallow dish in the shell. It fills its box before `rotate`, degrees.
A sculpted cap on a tall switch, whose LED follows the board's backlight and flares when it's hit. `profile` and `row` cut the cap as on `d-key="mech"`.
A low key on a scissor, whose legend and edge light follow the board's backlight.

A sculpted home-computer keycap: a dished top set back on a skirt, so a long front face looks up at you and carries a second legend. The label sits where a button's text would, so pad the button to lift it onto the top. `front` is the second legend, `height` how far the top stands up in mm, and `travel` how far it goes.

A key with a screen under it: a small panel fixed in the board, and a clear cap over it that goes down when pressed while the panel stays. A `<canvas>` inside is the panel, one canvas pixel to one of its pixels: draw on it and call `present`. `panel` is the side of what shows in mm, `radius` the corner of the hole, `gap` how far the cap stands off the hole's wall, `height` how far the cap stands proud and `travel` how far it goes, all in mm.

A big translucent pad over a lamp, on a pivot, in any outline: `path` and `viewbox` fill the box. `on` or a press lights it from behind, brightest over the lamp at `lamp`, mm from the box's top left. `pivot` is the way to the hinged side, degrees clockwise from up, and the far side drops `travel` mm. Leave it off and the whole pad goes straight down. `height` is mm above what it's on. Without a `path` it's its box with `radius` mm corners, as an illuminated pushbutton is, and the text inside is its legend.
A typewriter key: a paper disc under glass, in a metal ring, on a long throw.
Slivers of the side rail, coming out from behind the band, which hides the rest. Pressing one pushes it in. `material` is the rail's.

A phone key: silicone in the shape of its hole, with `num` big and `sub` small on it. `flip` sets them from the right, `inline` side by side, and `mark` is any other legend, in the key's `viewbox`. `on` turns the keypad light on under the mat.

A key that is a patch of one etched metal sheet over a snap dome, the sheet being whatever it sits on: no gap and no cap, only a groove etched through round it, and its legend, lit from under the sheet when `on`. `path` in `viewbox` is the groove's line, or a rounded box. `num`, `sub` and `mark` as on a phone key, `color` the light.
A square rubber pad to play with a finger, standing out of a well. It gives under a hit and comes back slowly. `material` is its rubber, `height` is mm and `travel` how far it gives.

A square tile of a keybed with a soft boss moulded on it, the whole thing on a rubber dome. `boss` is `round`, `pill` or `none`, and `cap` makes it another colour. `inlay` is a disc of another material set into the boss, `at` is how far across the tile the boss sits, 0 to 1, and `size` is its radius in mm. Sits in a well, which shows round it as a gap.
`d-key="piano black"` for a sharp. Heights are set so a row of them nests.

A short round pusher in the side of the case, pointing along `rot` from its box's left edge and middle, or for a pin from the edge it leaves by. Set `size`, its width in mm, and `out`, how far it stands in mm, for a plain pin. Or a stem with a head on it, lying along `rot` through the middle of its box: `stem` and `head` are each `across long` in mm, `band` is `long colour` round the head's waist and `at` how far up the head it starts in mm, `flutes` how many are cut round the head, `travel` how far it goes in, in mm. `material` is what it's made of.

The plain knob: turned aluminium over a thin skirt, with a spun top, a line to point with and its scale printed round it. Every form takes `grip` (smooth, knurled, ribbed, fluted, lobed) and `ribs` for how many, `top` (flat, spun, cap, dished, domed), `cap` and `face` for what the top is made of, `mark` (line, dot, arrow, slot, skirt, none) and `mark-color`, `pointer` for a wedge on a flat skirt, `from` and `to` for its stops in degrees, `height`, `taper` and `edge` in mm, `body` for the body's share of a skirted knob, `ticks`, `major`, `labels`, `sweep` and `size` for what's printed round it, `leds`, with `color`, for a ring of lamps that light up to where it points, and `ring` for a low boss moulded into the panel round it, with a groove round that and its scale printed on it.
The same on a click-stop switch: one click for each of `detents`, or each label, or each tick.
A moulded instrument knob: fluted body over a flat skirt with a line across it, and an aluminium disc let into the top.
The same on a click-stop switch.
A plain straight-sided moulded knob with a chamfered top.
The same on a click-stop switch, as a mode dial or a stepped encoder is.
The same on a shaft with no ends and no input: its `turn` attribute holds the angle, radians, for whatever it drives to read.
A tapered soft-touch knob with a coloured cap pressed on its top, held by a collet.
The same on a click-stop switch.
A fluted knob flaring into a cone at its foot, with a ray of ticks printed round it.
A slim ribbed stem with a domed top and a slot across it, on an endless encoder clicking at each step of its input.
A bar across a round foot, with a line along it to point with.
The same on a click-stop switch, as a selector is.

A pointer knob clicking between named positions. `labels` are printed around it. `leds` puts an LED at each position in place of its printed tick, and while it's `on` they all glow low and the one it points at burns, in `color`.
A big free-spinning wheel with a finger dimple, turned in circles.

A round knob with a knurled skirt and a smooth cap, turned by going round it. Its input runs from `from` to `to` degrees clockwise of straight up, which can be many turns, as a timer's is. `pitch` is the mm between teeth and `height` how far it stands, in mm. `cap` is how much of it the cap fills. `rings` cuts that many grooves round the cap. `legend` prints on the cap and turns with it, a slash starting a new line a step to the right, `size` mm tall and in `color`. `pointer` prints a white dot at the cap's edge.

A top-hat knob as on a guitar: a fine-ribbed barrel with a low domed top, its numbers round the edge of the top and turning with it. `legend` is printed across the middle. `count` is the highest number, `sweep` the degrees either side of straight up, `mark` the colour of the print, `material` the moulding, and `height` is mm.

A meter's function switch: a low disc with a bar moulded right across it, its long end past the rim and a white line let into the tip. The ribs run with the bar. A wafer switch, so it snaps between its positions, from `from` to `to` degrees clockwise of straight up. A press on either side of the middle clicks it one that way. The box is the sweep of the bar's tip. `size` is how much of that the disc fills, `ribs` the mm between ribs, 0 for none, and `height` and `grip` how far disc and bar stand, in mm.

A thread tension seen on its axis: a dished cup, the coil of the check spring, a numbered dial and the thumb nut that turns with it and runs in along the stud as it's tightened. Its input is the setting. `count` is the highest number, `sweep` the degrees either side of straight up, `mark` the colour of the numbers, `dial` what the dial is made of, `material` the cup and nut.

A winged pointer knob on a rotary switch: a round head with a pair of moulded wings under it, the longer one pointing, on a collar. It fills its box with the collar. `material` is the moulding, `collar` the metal round it, `mark` the line let into the pointing wing, `size` how much of the box the wings span, and `height` is mm.

A ribbed moulded knob with a smooth domed top and a short line at its foot to point with, turning a stepped switch. `size` is how much of its box it fills, and what's left shows `collar` if it has one. `lift` stands it that many mm up, on a `flange` of its own switch's outer shaft: it's the inner knob of a concentric pair. `cap` is its top, `mark` the line, `ribs` how many, and `height` how far it rises, mm.

The outer knob of a concentric pair: a low spun metal flange with a knurled rim and a line to point with, turning its own stepped switch. It fills its box. A `ribbed` knob with `lift` stands in the middle of it. `material` is the metal, `mark` the line, `knurl` how many teeth, `bore` how much of it the inner knob's well takes, and `height` is mm.

A jewel in a chrome bezel. `lens` is how the glass is cut: `jewel`, `dome`, `flat` or `fresnel`. `square` makes it a square pilot light, with a flat lens in a square bezel, and `bezel` names what the bezel is made of.

A neon indicator: a clear glass bulb in a black sleeve, with two electrodes inside, and when it's on the gas glows orange round them and nowhere else. Spec: an NE-2, 6mm across, with its electrodes about 1.5mm apart.
A small domed LED.
A pinhole in the panel: nothing to see until it is lit, unless `hole` drills it, so it shows dark when it's out.
Frosted glass with the lamp behind it: whatever it sits on, and lit through.
A flat bar of an LED, set level with what it sits in. It fills its box.

A warning tile on a panel: dark until it isn't, with its legend lit through it. `material` makes the tile that, with its legend always dark, as on a frosted tile with a bulb behind it, and `frame` is what holds it. `bare` is just a patch of phosphor laid into a panel, with its legend black on it.
One lit arrow for each way the car can go.
A ring of LEDs under a diffuser. `mode` says what it is doing, `level` how much of it is lit.

The light under a board of keys, one element in the device. `level` eases to its brightness, 0 to 1. `mode` is `wave`, `pulse`, `solid` or `off`, and `phase` is how far the colours have run. Paints first, so the keys read it as they paint.
A glass bulb in a hood, seen from the side. `on` lights it, and what's near it is lit too, out to `reach` mm, as strong as `gain`. `material` is the hood, whose lip is the top of its box.

A ribbed wheel showing through a slot, turned with a thumb. Each rib ticks past. `ribs` is how many go round it, `turns` how far it goes, and `height` how far it stands out of the slot, mm. `crown` is the height in mm of a big wheel standing out of a long slot and narrowing to each end, as a keyboard's bend wheel does, and `notch` cuts its middle position in it.
A rotary telephone dial. The input collects the digits. Going home it pulses once a digit, as the line did.
A ring with nothing of its own to see: the bezel or face of something round. `from` and `to` are its ends, in degrees.

A touch ring around a centre button. Stroking it steps the range, with a tick for each step. `legend` is how tall its legends stand, words and glyphs alike, mm, and `ink` what colour they're printed in.
Its disc is a real one on a bearing that you spin and that runs on after a flick. Its angle is in `turn`.
Its disc is fixed and feels a finger going round it, as `d-wheel="scroll"` does a hand.

A thumb disc let into a case, nearly flush, on a fixed hub with two pin holes. It carries a pointer and a raised pin for each angle in `pins`, degrees either side of it. Wraps a range input, with `from` and `to` its ends in degrees.

A knurled ring round a lens: a disc with teeth at its edge, seen from the front, turned with a hand on it. Stack them narrowest last and each one shows as a ring. `from` and `to` are its ends, in degrees.
With `clicks` it's a sprung ball in a row of dimples, as on an aperture ring: light, and hard to stop between.
A knurled drum seen from the side, on an upright axle, rolled sideways under a thumb through its stops.

A winding key seen from the front, coming out of the side of a case: a collar, a shaft, and a flat thumbpiece across the end of it. Drag up or down to wind it, one way only, against its pawl. The box starts at the side of the case and is as tall as the thumbpiece. A range holds the angle, 0 to 360.
A knurled wheel with most of itself behind the edge of a case, rolled along that edge with a thumb. `angle` is how far the edge slopes, degrees.

A handwheel on the end of a shaft that runs across the view, so it's seen nearly edge on: an ellipse, its near side to the right. Pull the near side down to turn it, and it runs on a little, being heavy. Its box is the wheel and the rim that stands off it by `rim-off` mm. `lean` is how wide the ellipse is for its height, `holes` how many are cut through the web, `material` the casting and `rim` the ring round it.

A heavy disc on a bearing, driven from under by a small motor, and free to be caught. `rpm` is where the motor is headed. Flick it and it runs on. Hold it and the motor gives way. `hub` is the dished centre, `pins` the screws in it, `path` and `viewbox` are art printed across the whole disc, and `marks` are words on it, which turn with it.

A crank on a shaft coming out of the side of a case, turned round and round. Two inputs: a range holds the angle from 0 to 360, 0 with the arm laid up the side, and a checkbox whether it's folded out. A hand goes round the shaft, and how far it is to the right of it stands for how far the grip has come towards you. Folding it away takes the arm home first. `reach` is the arm and `pivot` the shaft's height in the box, both mm. The box starts at the side of the case and has to take the swing.
A handle of five spokes. Held by the lock it gives a little and comes back.

A knurled crown seen from above, standing out of the case at three o'clock. Drag it up or down to turn it, and out or in to pull it to its positions. The first input is what turning it sets, and the second where it's pulled to, from 0 pushed in: `max="2"` for a crown that winds, sets the date and sets the time. A checkbox after them makes it screw down: ticked, it's screwed to the case and can't be pulled. Turn it back to unscrew it, and it springs out to winding. To screw it down again, push it in as you turn it on.

A ribbed cap on a range input, sliding in a sunk slot between printed ticks. It runs across when its box is wider than tall. `slot` is the slot's width, `cap` the cap's across the slot and `tick-length` how long a tick is, all in mm. `d-slider="fader fin"` tops it with a thin blade, as on a synth, and `fader flat` with a low square, as on a DJ mixer. `leds` puts a row of that many LEDs beside the slot in place of its ticks, a level meter: while it's `on` they glow low, and up to the cap they burn, in `color`.

A knob on a rod, drawn out of the end of a body and pulled back in by its spring when it's let go, as a choke or a starter cord is. The box is the knob home against the body, which the rod comes out of on the left. `travel` is how far it draws and `rod` the rod's diameter, both mm. `path` is the knob's outline seen from the side in its `viewbox`, a ball on a neck if there's none; it's turned, so round all the way round.

A T-handle on a stem, pulled straight down, and caught by a pawl at the bottom so it stays pulled until its input is set back, as a fire alarm's is. Short of the pawl its spring takes it back. The box is the handle home, with the bar along its bottom. `travel` is how far it pulls, `bar` the bar's depth, `stem` the stem's width and `height` how far the bar stands, all mm. `text` is moulded along the bar, in `color`.
A long lever in a slot, topped with a ball.

A ribbed nub in a slot. Works with a checkbox, or a range for three or more positions. `pill` rounds the slot's ends, `nub` is how much of it the nub fills, and `mark` prints a dot of that colour on the nub. `fin` makes the nub a low plate with a raised ridge across it, for a thumb, and `plain` leaves its ribs off. `lit` puts a lamp behind the slot, which fills as the nub slides over. `height` is how far the nub stands, mm.
A strip you touch anywhere along. `segments` lights dots, or 0 for a solid bar.
An analog trigger behind the rocker. It travels with a drag and springs back on release.
A ribbed nub coming out of the top edge of a case, which closes over the rest of it. A checkbox holds which end it's at, and its box is the slot it runs in.

A plate with a slot and a scale, and a wing screw that slides along the slot to set a length, as a stitch regulator has. Its input is the setting, its top end up. Its box is the plate. `ends` is mm from each end of the box to where the wing can get, `left` and `right` the scales printed down each side of the slot, top first, `mark` their colour, `material` the plate, and `reach` how far the screw's tail hangs, x y in mm.
A joystick. Wrap two range inputs, across then up, and it sprints back to the middle.
A thumbstick: a hollow rubber cap on a short post, in a rounded well.
A thin stem with a knurled head over an open gimbal, as on a radio transmitter. It stands in a slotted cup, and each axis slides its own plate along under the window.
A small five-way nub, pitted so a thumb stays on it.
A slide pad: a flat disc that doesn't tilt but slides across a shallow round well, as on a handheld. Its top is dished for the thumb, and `ring` on adds the raised rim some have round that dish.
A short paddle standing out of a long slot, sprung to the middle, for bending a note. It rocks along the slot on a range input. `lean` is how much of the slot it can reach, 0 to 1.
A pad you touch anywhere, for two values at once. Wrap two range inputs, across then up.

`disc` for a dished disc on a pivot, `ring` for a round moulding with raised arrows and a hole for a centre key, `cross` for one moulding with a dimple and ribbed arms. On a cross, `arm` is how wide each arm is, mm, `smooth` leaves the ribs off and keeps the dimple, and `plain` leaves both off. `flat` is a flat ring let into its face with a hub of its own in the middle, as on a music player with no wheel. `hub` is how wide that is, mm, `center` its material, `labels` the ring's legends clockwise from the top, `legend` how tall they stand, mm, and `ink` their colour. `mark` prints one on the hub, `mark-size` tall, mm, in `mark-ink`.

A mouse that rolls about its box under the hand, the body filling only part of that box. Holds two range inputs, across then down, 0 to 1, and a button for each of its three keys. `size` is the body in mm, `key-material` its keys, and `cord` the point the wire runs off to, in mm from the box's corner.
A bat handle through a collar, on a checkbox. It flips up and down.
A toggle sprung to its centre, which is off, with a momentary contact each way. It wraps a range of 0, 1 and 2: up reads 2, down reads 0, and it comes back to 1.
A toggle that stays where it's thrown, on a range: two positions or more, the highest at the top, with a click at each.
The same toggle on its side, thrown left and right, the highest value to the right. Give it a wide box.

A rocker in a frame, tipped by a checkbox. `lit` puts a lamp in the on side, or under both with `whole`, and `glow` is how bright. `bare` is a plain paddle in a slot, with no frame and no marks. `blank` is the frame with no marks, for a panel that prints its own. `cap` is the rocker's material where it isn't the frame's, `frame` the frame's width in mm, and `flip` puts on at the bottom end.
The same rocker on its side, tipping left and right.

A barrel lock seen from the front, filling its box, with a key standing straight out of it, so all that shows of the key is the edge of its bow. `material` is the collar and `core` the barrel. `key` is the key's material, or `none` for a lock with the key out, whose barrel still turns. `height` is how far the key stands, mm. `labels` are printed outside the box: off above, on to the right.
A sprung lever on a round foot, flicked over with a fingertip and back on its own when let go. `rest` is its lean in degrees, `inset` what fills its blade.

A blade switch: a lever through a slot, clicking through each step of its input, with its pin out of sight under the panel. `pin` is where it turns, x y in mm from its top left, and `from` and `to` are the ends of its swing, degrees from straight up round that pin. `material` is the tip and `height` how far it stands, mm.

A moulded key on a pivot with two ends, each a real button placed in its box. `path`, `viewbox`, `mark` as on a phone key, and `dips` the two ends, as x y pairs in the viewbox. It turns on the point halfway between them.

A long bar on a pin, rocked in the plane of its face, that goes back to the middle when let go. Filling its box, with `pin` as x, y in mm from the top left, which is also where the riveted end of the pin shows.
A hinged safety cover. What it guards can only be reached with the cover up.

A clear acrylic lid hinged along the top of its box, seen from above, so opening it closes it up towards the hinge until it stands past upright, edge on, and leaves nothing over what it covered. Put a button in it, last of all. Shut, it's in the way. Open, only the strip of it standing up can be reached.
A shallow cap in a frame, with `inset` let into its top. Click it and it lifts clear on its hinge, `lift` mm. `inset`'s margins are `margin`, mm: top, right, bottom, left.
A cap that fits the top of a case, square where they meet, on a pin at its bottom left corner.
A cooking ring: printed on the glass, with a coil under it that shows through as it heats.
Which ring a row of controls belongs to: a small printed plan of the top.
A digit that is not there until it is lit. Nothing prints on the glass when `value` is empty.
A bar handle on two posts. Pressing it pulls the door out of its seal, and again closes it.
The doors, with the landing behind them. `open` slides them apart, `floor` names the landing.

The tape's whole route: tension arms, guides, three heads, the capstan and its pinch roller. `reels` is the left x, right x, y and radius of the two reels, and `line` the height of the tape past the heads, all mm from the part's corner. `left` and `right` are how full each reel is, and `play` and `moving` what the transport is doing.
A tape reel. `spin` is turns per second and `fill` how much tape it holds, 0 to 1.

A cassette behind a window, with its hubs one above the other. `spin` is turns a second at the fuller hub, and it gets there and stops the way a tape does, not at once. `axle` is how far in from the left the hubs sit.

A turntable platter, with a three armed spindle and marks to see it turn by. `rpm` is where it's headed, and it's heavy, so it takes its time to get there and to stop, unless `rise` gives the seconds its motor takes. `d-turntable="platter strobe"` is a deck's platter instead: rows of strobe dots round a dark band, a bright chamfer, a ribbed mat, and a record on it with `label` for the material of its label and `words` the two lines printed on that. `strobe` is each row's radius:count:dot radius, in mm.

A moulded pickup arm on a pin, resting along +y. `pivot` is the pin's x, y in mm from the top left and `length` is pin to stylus in mm. Wraps a range input, whose ends are the rest and the end of the record, `sweep` degrees on. `d-turntable="tonearm s"` is a deck's arm: a bent tube with a headshell and cartridge, a gimbal, and a counterweight behind the pin.

Drawn tubing, round all the way, along a path. `points` is x y r for each corner, mm from its top left, r being the radius of the bend there; `size` is its outside diameter, mm. `rings` are the ferrules round it, each a distance along the path, mm, in `ring` (`width proud`, mm, and `ring-material`). `material` is the tube, and `height` how far its top stands, mm.

The flare of a horn, as a body turned on an axis along the middle of its box. `profile` is its radius at each distance along from the box's left edge, in pairs, mm: `distance radius`. What's nested in it sits on its curve. `material` is the metal, and `height` how far its widest stands, mm.

A piston in its casing, seen side on with the button at the top of its box: a button on a stem, a domed top cap, the casing and its band, and a knurled bottom cap. Pressing runs the button and stem down the casing. It says so with a `valve` event, with `down`. `size` is the casing's outside diameter, `travel` how far it goes, and `stem`, `cap`, `band` and `foot` where each starts down the box, mm. `material` is the casing and top cap, `foot-material` the bottom cap, `button` the rim of the finger button, `pearl` the inlay on it, `rod` the stem, and `height` how far the casing's top stands, mm.

A sprung lever that holds a cork against a hole in the tube, to let the water out. Its pivot is `pin`, x y mm from its top left. `points` is its bent arm, x y r for each corner, mm from its top left, and pressing lifts it round the pin by `swing` degrees. It says so with a `valve` event. `material` is the lever and `height` how far it stands, mm.
A ring soldered on for a finger to pull a slide by, filling its box. `size` is the rod, mm. `material` is the metal and `height` how far it stands, mm.

A stay between two tubes: a rod through its box from top to bottom, ending in a pointed foot at each end where it's soldered on. `size` is the rod and `foot` the width of the feet, mm. `material` is the metal and `height` how far it stands, mm.

A whole deck, in `card="Q hearts"` buttons in the order they lie, bottom first, with the `grip`s a hand takes the stack by. The top card takes a tap and it's dealt to the next of `deal`, x y pairs in mm from the deck's middle, the last of them taking the rest. A loose one turns over at a tap and goes where it's dragged, and back on the stack if it's let go over it. `grip="cut"` lifts the top off, `grip="spread"` fans them, a range from 0 to 1, `grip="over"` turns the lot, and `grip="take"` and `grip="away"` get them out of the box and back in. With a `d-cards="box"` inside, it starts in that, and draws it. Size it to one card. `material` is left to the pack: a card is what it is.
The carton a deck comes in. Inside a deck, the deck draws it, as the cards go in and out of it; on its own it draws itself.
The box's end, tucked in. A tap pulls it out, or shuts it again. Sits along the top of a `d-cards="box"`, and draws upwards out of it.

A rod on a pin below it, going from side to side, with a weight clipped to it that sets how fast. Two inputs: a range for which mark the weight is on and a checkbox for whether it's going. `marks` is beats a minute and mm down the box for each, top first, which is how an uneven scale reads. The weight's top edge is what points at them. `x` and `pivot` place the pin in mm, `reach` is the rod's length, and `swing` its degrees each way. Set it going with a click on the rod. `wound` is the seconds of spring left, or it runs for ever. `height` is how far the rod stands off what it's on, in mm. Put what hides its foot after it.

The sprung sheet over a floppy disk's head opening, filling its box at rest. A hole through the sheet, `window` in mm from the box's top left as `x y w h`, sits over solid case until the sheet runs `travel` mm, negative for leftwards, and the hole comes over an opening onto the film inside. Let go, it springs shut. `height` is how far it stands, mm.

The steel hub of a floppy disk in its round opening in the case, which fills the box, and turns with a hand. A spindle goes in the square hole at its middle and a drive pin in the oblong one off to the side. `hub` is the steel's diameter, mm.

The chips on a wafer before it's sawn, as many whole ones as fit a disc as wide as the box and inside the box, so a flat cut across the wafer takes its row off. Each is a sheet of oxide, in `material`, with memory arrays ruled so fine they split a lamp into its colours (`array`), a block of logic (`logic`) and pads round its edge (`pads`). `die` is a chip's `w h`, `street` the gap sawn away between them and `edge` how far in from the rim they stop, all mm.
The gold contacts of a smart card or SIM, filling its box: a plate let into the card and split by fine channels into eight pads round a middle.

A plane of a case falling away towards one edge of its box, `drop` mm by the time it gets there, and staying down past it to the edge of the surface it's nested in, if it is. `side` is `top`, `right`, `bottom` or `left`.

A course of strings over a bridge and a nut. Catch one and let go, or sweep across them: each says so with a `pluck` event, and is a real button for the keyboard. `bridge` and `nut` are where each string leaves off, x y in mm from its top left, `heads` where it goes past the nut, and `gauges` how thick each is, mm. The first `wound` of them are wound in `wrap`. `material` is the plain wire, and `height` how far they stand off whatever is under them, mm, following it, as a shadow from their true height would lie further off than it reads.

The frets, dots and nut on a neck, from a fretboard that fills its box: the nut along its right edge and the heel along its left. `scale` is the string's length, `count` how many frets, and `nut` and `heel` how wide the board is at each end, mm. `material` is the fretwire, `dot` the colour of the inlays, `at` the frets they mark, with two at the octaves.

A single coil under a moulded cover, its six pole pieces standing through it. `rotate` slants it, degrees. `stagger` is how far each pole stands, mm, `pitch` their spacing, mm. `material` is the cover, `pole` the metal, and `height` how far the cover stands, mm.

A vintage tremolo bridge, seen from above: a steel plate with six bent saddles on it, a row of pivot screws and the socket for the arm. Its box is the plate, stepped back at one corner. `material` is the steel, `pitch` the distance between strings, `at` how far along the plate the saddles sit, and `screws` how far along their row of screws, mm. `height` is how far the saddles stand, mm.

A bent rod with a tip, out of a tremolo's socket and across the guitar. `points` is its path, x y in mm from its top left, with the tip on the last stretch of it. `material` is the rod, `tip` its end, `height` how far it stands, mm.

A machine head from the front: the post a string winds on, in its bushing, on a box centred on the post. `button` is where the turning button shows past the edge of the headstock, x y in mm from the post, and `button-size` its width, mm. `material` is the metal, `height` how far the post stands, mm.

Boards under whatever stands in it, one to a line, however the page wrapped it, in the gap below that line. `case` is a bookcase, with a top and two sides in the padding and empty boards down to the bottom. `wall` is boards alone, as on brackets. `board` is how thick one is and `side` how wide the sides are, in mm, and `height` how far they stand off the back.

A hardback, filling its box. `face` shows its cover, with whatever's stamped on it nested inside, and `spine` stands with its back out and its words up it. Pulling it toward you is the press: it comes out a little under a resting hand, and further when it's held. `height` is how far it stands, in mm.

Bricks in mortar, filling the box, cut where it cuts them. The value is the bond: `stretcher` lays them long and breaks each joint on the course below, `soldier` stands them on end in one course. `brick`, `course` and `joint` are the size of one, in mm. A UK brick is the default: 215 by 65 with a 10 joint, spec. `height` is how far its face stands off the mortar.
A hole in a wall, as deep as the wall's outer skin, so what's set in it stands back from the face. `depth` is how far, and the floor is what shows if nothing is nested in it.

A window: a fixed frame, a sash in each light and glass behind them, filling its box. `lights` is how many, side by side. `frame` and `sash` are how wide they are, in mm, and `height` how far the frame stands off the glass.

A sill under an opening: it comes out past the wall by `height`, back into the opening by `depth`, and its top falls toward the front. It runs past the opening at each end, by `stool` mm, and those ends are left flat for the brickwork to bear on. The box is the whole of it.

The moving top of a typewriter: platen, paper, lever and knobs. `col` and `row` drive it. `pitch` and `leading` are the mm a letter and a line move, `cols` how many letters fit, and the element's `lines` what's typed.
The basket of type bars. `bar` says which one is flying up to the paper.
A small bell with a hammer. `ring` swings it, and `lit` is there for when motion is off.
The moulded case, dished around the dial, with the cradle and its two hook plungers. `dial` and `cord` are where those sit, mm from the case's corner.

The handset and its coiled cord. Drawn from circles and rotated bars, so swinging it costs no fields. It covers the whole desk. `cradle`, `rest` and `cord` are the points it hangs on, lies at and runs back to, mm from the part's corner.

What the lever stands in: a brass plate with the middle out of it, screwed down, two posts, the leaf that carries the fixed contact, and the trunnion screws either side with their lock nuts. The box is the plate. `material` is its brass.

A flat black knob on an open lever, which rocks on the trunnion's points and comes back on its spring. Press it and the lever's contact comes down on the stud. The box is the knob, and the lever runs off it to the right. `reach` is how far the axis is from the knob's middle, mm, and `arm` what the lever's made of.

The circuit closer: a curved strip of brass on a pin, with a ball on its end, thrown across to short the contacts and hold the line closed. Open is at the ball's furthest from the lever. The box runs from the ball at its bottom left to just past the pin at its top right, and the strip and ball are what take the hand. `material` is the strip.

The wheel of an embosser: a ribbed disc with its characters round a printed face, clicking from each to the next and round past the end. The input runs from 0 to as many characters as there are, whose ends are the same place. `chars` runs clockwise, a space being the blank that spaces words and shown as a dot. `index` is where the chosen one sits, degrees clockwise from the top. `material` is the disc and `face` what's printed on, `face-size` how wide it is and `ring` how far out its characters sit, `legend` how tall they are, all mm. `height` is mm.

The same wheel's edge where it comes up through a slot in the top of the case, seen from above, so it fills the slot as a shallow arch and goes round with the wheel. `of` picks the wheel in its device. It draws its slot too. `material` and `face` are the disc and the printed face, `height` how far it stands, mm.

The squeeze handle of an embosser, swinging on a pin at its far end towards the grip: all the way in and it strikes, which fires a bubbling `squeeze`, and on the way home it's `squeeze-back`, which feeds the tape. Short of that nothing happens, as with the real thing. Its box is where you get hold of it. `path` is its outline, in mm from that box's corner, and it can run far outside it, with `extent` the x y w h it fills, and `nose` is a narrower piece of it with a tighter edge. `pin` is where it turns and `swing` how many degrees it goes, `material` what it's made of, `height` mm, `crown` how much it swells, mm.

The cutter of an embosser: a tab you push in, and a blade it drives across the tape at the end of its stroke, which fires a bubbling `cut`. The tab fills its box. `blade` is where the blade runs, x and then the y it starts and ends at, mm from the box's corner, `travel` how far the tab goes, mm, `material` the tab, `height` mm.

The tape of an embosser, in the run from where it's punched to the air outside: its box runs along the tape, as wide as the tape, ending on the right at the punch. It lies on whatever's under it and can hang past the device. It's what wires the embosser up: on a `squeeze` in its device it takes the character at the wheel's index, on the way back it feeds on, and on a `cut` it parts at the blade and the end falls away to the tray. `letters` is what's on it so far, `lead` the mm of blank before them, `pitch` the mm a letter takes, `cap` how tall a letter is, mm. `blade` is how far along its box the cutter is, `tray` where the first piece lands, x y mm from its corner, and `leading` the mm between pieces. `material` is the tape.

A sprung clip on the back of a thing, filling its box: one sheet standing off the back, pinned across at one end, which a thumb on that end lifts at the other. A press on its button opens it. `hinge` says which end, top or bottom, `radius` rounds its corners and `height` is how far it stands, mm. `mark` engraves a path across its middle, `mark-size` wide, mm, in a square `viewbox` of that path's.
The holes of a wind guard, pressed through whatever it's on, and the two folds down its sides. `rows` is how many holes in each row, and the rows sit half a pitch out of step.
A knurled wheel, filling its box. It turns on an axle held by whatever passes in front of it.
A leaf of sprung steel riveted through the middle of its box. It rides the joint named by `of`, and tips over as that opens.

The barrel that twists off: drag up or down across it. `profile` is its section, stations of `x r` in mm from its left. `thread` and `off` are how far the thread carries it, and how far off it has to go, mm. `lay` is how its brushing runs, degrees from along it. `material` is the steel.

The button on the end that works the cam: press it, and it stays in, and press it again. `aria-pressed` on its button says it's in. `profile` is its section, `travel` how far it goes to the bottom, mm. `material` is the steel.

The fixed half of the barrel, with the ring at its end that holds the clip. `profile` is its section and `collar` the ring's, as stations from its left. `legend` is cut round it at `legend-at`, mm from its left, `legend-size` high. `material` is the steel, `ring` the metal of the collar.

A sprung clip, seen from the front, standing off whatever's under it. `path` is its outline in mm on its box. `feathers` are where a slanted groove crosses it, x and half width in mm from its left, and `spine` where the groove along it runs, x to x. `material` is the metal, `height` how far it stands, mm.

What the barrel hides: the refill and its spring, and the thread the barrel runs on, which stays with the other half. `clicker` names the button that pushes it, `travel` how far that moves it at the bottom, mm. `nose` and `tube` are the refill's section as stations from its left. `thread` is where the thread is, `x x r`. `spring` is `seat free radius`: the barrel's seat for it, its free length and its radius, mm, and it sits on the refill's shoulder where the nose meets the tube. `material` is the tube, `tip` the nose.
A strip of grit on what it's glued to. `struck` is where it's been struck so far, as x y x y in mm from its top left, four to a stroke: each scrapes the grit pale.

One tooth of a comb of matches, standing where it's stapled at the foot of its box. `torn` is mm from the foot where it was torn out, and what's left is a ragged stub. `head` and `material` say what it's dipped in and made of.
A match out of its comb, head at the top of its box, torn off at the foot. `burn` is how far it's burnt from the head, 0 to 1, and `spent` that its head has gone, with it lit or not.

A needle bar coming down out of the head, its clamp and the needle in it. `of` names what turns it, and it's at the top of its stroke with the shaft at 0. It stops at `plate`, mm below its box's top, where the needle goes through. `stroke` is how far it runs, `bar` how much of it shows at the top, `length` the needle, all mm. `thread` is where the thread comes down from, x y in mm from its top left, and `cotton` what the thread is.

A thread take-up seen edge on: the lever nodding in a slot in the head, ahead of the needle. Its box is the slot. `of` names what turns it, `lead` how far ahead it runs, degrees, `reach` how far its eye stands out of the slot's left side, mm. `from` and `to` are where the thread comes from and goes to, x y in mm from its top left, `cotton` what the thread is, and `material` the lever.

The toothed feed that walks the cloth along: up through its slot, along, down and back, with the needle out of the way. Its box is the slot. `of` names what turns it and `by` what sets how far it walks, whose top end is the shortest stitch. `walk` is how far it goes at the longest setting, as it shows, mm, and `teeth` how many rows it has.

A presser foot on its bar: down on the plate, up off it. Click it, or push it. Its box runs from where the bar leaves the head down to the plate. `bar` is how far the bar sits along the box, `shank` how far the foot's shank, `shin` how far down the box the bar stops and `sole` where the sole begins, all mm, and `lift` how far it comes up. `material` is the foot.

A spear blade on a pin. It lies along its box and swings half a turn in the plane of the face, back first, and the handle closes over it. Ground from a line down the middle to the edge, with a nick for a nail by the back. `stamp` is what's struck in the tang, with `|` between lines, reading from the tip.

A slim tool living in a slot, which draws out past the end of its box. `d-tool="pull tweezers"`, or `pull pick` for a tapered stick. `end` is the radius of its head in mm, so it can take the curve of the handle it finishes.
The door in its frame. `open` runs from 0, bolts home, to 1, bolts drawn in.
The cushion a watch sits on in a box, rolling away at both ends. `flat` and `roll` are mm from its middle, and `fall` is how far it drops. What's nested in it sits on top.
A padded strap, drawn flat and rolled over the cushion. The edge is painted, the flange holds the stitching, and the pad swells up inside it.

A strap moulded in one piece of resin or rubber, rolled away past `flat` mm from the case over `roll` mm, falling `fall` mm. It runs up the page, or down with `tail`. `pitch` is mm between its ribs, `slot` the length and width in mm of the slot across the middle of each. `edge` is the rounded edge in mm, `height` mm.

A metal bracelet, drawn flat and rolled over the cushion as a strap is. It runs from the case along its box, up the page, or down with `tail`, and narrows to `end` mm wide. `links` is `rows`, three pieces a row with the middle one half a link out of step, or `bars`, wide bars with a polished link across each joint. `pitch` is a link in mm, and `flat`, `roll` and `fall` are mm from the case end to the bend. `rise` is how high in mm the end link stands where it meets the case, curving down to the rest over its length. `fold` is a radius in mm: past `flat` it goes over that curve and away, its links shortening as they turn.

One piece of steel: the barrel and whatever holds the strap. `path` and `viewbox` give its outline, or it's a round barrel with curved lugs. `height` is mm over what it sits on, `camber` how far the lugs fall along the wrist, and `polished` a bright edge in mm. `lugs` is the gap between them in mm, for a strap running up and down the page: the sides facing it are cut sharp and brushed to the edge. It's brushed round the dial, unless `lay` says otherwise.

A bezel that stays put. `square` rounds it off a square, 2 being a circle, and `inner` does the same for the `opening` in it, in mm. `height`, `floor` for how far the dial lies below what it sits on, `wall` for the slope down to it, `edge` for a polished edge in mm, `flat` to cut that edge straight and not round it, and `top` for a flat band of some material inside that. `material` is the bezel itself, polished steel unless it says.

A bezel with a coin edge and a printed insert of minutes, that clicks round one way only. `clicks` is how many times to the turn, `teeth` how many scoops are cut round its edge, `material` the insert, and the rest as for `d-watch="bezel"`. Drawn at 41mm and scaled.

A dial, the shape of the opening it lies in. `square` as for a bezel. `markers` is `batons`, with `index` their length and width as units of 206 across and `skip` the hours left out, `round`, with a triangle at 12 and bars at 6 and 9, or `none`. `track` is `ticks`, `beads` or `none`, for a dial whose scales are printed on it by `d-mark="scale"`. `date` is the hour a date window sits at, `date-at` how far out from 0 to 1, `date-size` how big it's cut. `ribs` is the pitch in mm of embossed lines across it, `bright` a colour shading out from the middle over a `material` that's darker, and `registers` adds two small dials. What's nested in it sits on it.

Hands on real heights above the dial, which follow the clock. `d-watch="hands spoke"` or `hands baton` tell the time, and the seconds sweep at eight beats a second. Without one they're a chronograph's: blued, with a red hand and two small registers, driven by `since` and `spent`. `offset` is minutes ahead of the clock. `hands stop` are a stopwatch's, also driven by `since` and `spent`: no time of day, just a long hand that beats five times a second, ticking as it goes, and a small one on a register. `lap` is seconds for the long hand's turn, `minutes` minutes for the small hand's, and `register` where that one's centre is, `x y` in mm from the long hand's. The box is the sweep of the long hand's tip, and `reach` the small hand in mm. With neither `since` nor `spent` they fly back by the short way, as a heart cam sends them.
